label: External conditions alone cannot explain complex coadaptations
statement: Complex adaptations and coadaptations between organisms, such as the woodpecker's feeding structures or the misseltoe's dependence on particular trees, birds and insects, cannot be accounted for by the direct effects of external conditions such as climate and food.
quote: it is preposterous to attribute to mere external conditions, the structure, for instance, of the woodpecker, with its feet, tail, beak, and tongue, so admirably adapted to catch insects under the bark of trees.
scope: adapted structures of animals and plants, especially those involving relations with other species

label: Overproduction plus slight profitable variation leads to natural selection
statement: Because more individuals of each species are born than can survive, there is a recurring struggle for existence, so any individual that varies even slightly in a way profitable to itself has a better chance of surviving and thus of being naturally selected.
quote: As many more individuals of each species are born than can possibly survive; and as, consequently, there is a frequently recurring struggle for existence, it follows that any being, if it vary however slightly in any manner profitable to itself, under the complex and sometimes varying conditions of life, will have a better chance of surviving, and thus be _naturally selected_.
scope: all animals and plants

label: Natural selection causes extinction of less improved forms and divergence
statement: Natural selection almost inevitably causes much extinction of less improved forms of life and produces divergence of character.
quote: we shall then see how Natural Selection almost inevitably causes much Extinction of the less improved forms of life and induces what I have called Divergence of Character.
scope: all organic beings over evolutionary time

label: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species
statement: Species are not independently created and immutable; species of the same genus are lineal descendants of some other, generally extinct, species, just as varieties of one species descend from that species.
quote: I am fully convinced that species are not immutable; but that those belonging to what are called the same genera are lineal descendants of some other and generally extinct species, in the same manner as the acknowledged varieties of any one species are the descendants of that species.
scope: all species of plants and animals

label: Natural selection is the main but not exclusive means of modification
statement: Natural selection has been the main, but not the only, cause of the modification of species.
quote: Furthermore, I am convinced that Natural Selection has been the main but not exclusive means of modification.
scope: all organic beings

label: Domesticated forms vary more among individuals than wild species do
statement: Individuals of the same variety of long-cultivated plants and domesticated animals generally differ much more from each other than individuals of any one species or variety in nature.
quote: they generally differ much more from each other, than do the individuals of any one species or variety in a state of nature.
scope: older cultivated plants and domesticated animals compared with wild species

label: Greater domestic variability is caused by changed, less uniform conditions
statement: The greater variability of domestic productions is due to their being raised under conditions of life less uniform than, and somewhat different from, those of their parent species in nature.
quote: I think we are driven to conclude that this greater variability is simply due to our domestic productions having been raised under conditions of life not so uniform as, and somewhat different from, those to which the parent-species have been exposed under nature.
scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants

label: Variability arises mainly from effects on reproductive elements before conception
statement: The most frequent cause of variability is that the male and female reproductive elements have been affected by the conditions of life before conception, the reproductive system being more sensitive to changed conditions than any other part of the organisation.
quote: But I am strongly inclined to suspect that the most frequent cause of variability may be attributed to the male and female reproductive elements having been affected prior to the act of conception.
scope: animals and plants under domestication or confinement

label: Inherited effects of use and disuse modify domestic animals
statement: Habitual use and disuse of parts produce inherited changes in domestic animals; for example, domestic ducks have lighter wing bones and heavier leg bones relative to the skeleton than wild ducks because they fly less and walk more.
quote: I find in the domestic duck that the bones of the wing weigh less and the bones of the leg more, in proportion to the whole skeleton, than do the same bones in the wild-duck; and I presume that this change may be safely attributed to the domestic duck flying much less, and walking more, than its wild parent.
scope: domesticated animals

label: Selecting one trait unconsciously modifies other correlated parts
statement: Because of laws of correlation of growth, when man selects for and augments any peculiarity, he almost certainly also modifies other parts of the structure without intending to.
quote: Hence, if man goes on selecting, and thus augmenting, any peculiarity, he will almost certainly unconsciously modify other parts of the structure, owing to the mysterious laws of the correlation of growth.
scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants under artificial selection

label: Inherited peculiarities appear in offspring at the age they appeared in parent
statement: A peculiarity tends to appear in the offspring at the same period of life at which it first appeared in the parent, though sometimes earlier.
quote: A much more important rule, which I think may be trusted, is that, at whatever period of life a peculiarity first appears, it tends to appear in the offspring at a corresponding age, though sometimes earlier.
scope: domesticated animals and plants, extended to organisms generally

label: Domestic races differ like congeneric species, but usually less
statement: Apart from their lesser uniformity, their often monstrous development of one part, and their fertility when crossed, domestic races of a species differ from each other in the same manner as closely allied species of a genus in nature, though in most cases to a lesser degree.
quote: domestic races of the same species differ from each other in the same manner as, only in most cases in a lesser degree than, do closely-allied species of the same genus in a state of nature.
scope: domestic races compared with closely allied wild congeneric species

label: Any wild species domesticated as long would vary as much as existing domestics
statement: Domesticated species were not chosen for an unusual inherent tendency to vary; any comparable set of wild animals and plants, bred under domestication for as many generations, would on average vary as much as the parent species of existing domesticated productions have.
quote: I cannot doubt that if other animals and plants, equal in number to our domesticated productions, and belonging to equally diverse classes and countries, were taken from a state of nature, and could be made to breed for an equal number of generations under domestication, they would vary on an average as largely as the parent species of our existing domesticated productions have varied.
scope: wild animals and plants brought into domestication

label: Domestic dogs descend from several wild species
statement: Domestic dogs have probably descended from several distinct wild species rather than from a single one.
quote: from geographical and other considerations, I think it highly probable that our domestic dogs have descended from several wild species.
scope: domestic dogs and wild Canidae

label: All domestic pigeon breeds descend from the rock-pigeon
statement: All domestic pigeon breeds, however different, have descended from the rock-pigeon (Columba livia) and its geographical sub-species, not from several aboriginal wild stocks.
quote: I can feel no doubt that all our domestic breeds have descended from the Columba livia with its geographical sub-species.
scope: domestic pigeon breeds

label: Domestic breeds arise mainly by man's accumulation of successive variations
statement: Domestic breeds were not produced suddenly in their present useful form; their key cause is man's accumulative selection, nature supplying successive variations and man adding them up in directions useful to him.
quote: The key is man’s power of accumulative selection: nature gives successive variations; man adds them up in certain directions useful to him.
scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants

label: Races differ most in the parts man selects
statement: Continued selection of slight variations in one part valued by man, such as leaves, flowers or fruit, produces races that differ from each other chiefly in that part, while other parts differ only slightly.
quote: as a general rule, I cannot doubt that the continued selection of slight variations, either in the leaves, the flowers, or the fruit, will produce races differing from each other chiefly in these characters.
scope: cultivated plant varieties within a species

label: Unconscious selection over centuries modifies any breed
statement: Unconscious selection, in which people simply breed from their best animals without aiming to change the breed, would over centuries improve and modify any breed, as methodical breeders have done within their lifetimes.
quote: Nevertheless I cannot doubt that this process, continued during centuries, would improve and modify any breed, in the same way as Bakewell, Collins, etc., by this very same process, only carried on more methodically, did greatly modify, even during their own lifetimes, the forms and qualities of their cattle.
scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants

label: Slow accumulated change hides the wild parents of old cultivated plants
statement: Because a large amount of change has been slowly and unconsciously accumulated in long-cultivated plants, in many cases their wild parent-stocks can no longer be recognised.
quote: A large amount of change in our cultivated plants, thus slowly and unconsciously accumulated, explains, as I believe, the well-known fact, that in a vast number of cases we cannot recognise, and therefore do not know, the wild parent-stocks of the plants which have been longest cultivated in our flower and kitchen gardens.
scope: long-cultivated garden and crop plants

label: Domestic races differ greatly externally but little internally
statement: Because man can select mainly on externally visible deviations, domestic races differ greatly in external characters and relatively slightly in internal parts or organs.
quote: We can, I think, further understand the frequently abnormal character of our domestic races, and likewise their differences being so great in external characters and relatively so slight in internal parts or organs.
scope: domestic races of animals

label: Keeping large numbers of individuals favours successful selection
statement: Because useful variations appear only occasionally, keeping a large number of individuals greatly increases the chance of useful variations appearing and is of the highest importance to success in selection.
quote: But as variations manifestly useful or pleasing to man appear only occasionally, the chance of their appearance will be much increased by a large number of individuals being kept; and hence this comes to be of the highest importance to success.
scope: artificial selection on domesticated animals and plants

label: Accumulative selection is the predominant cause of change in domestic races
statement: Among the causes of change in domestic races, including conditions of life, use and disuse, correlation and crossing, the accumulative action of selection, whether methodical or unconscious, is by far the predominant power.
quote: Over all these causes of Change I am convinced that the accumulative action of Selection, whether applied methodically and more quickly, or unconsciously and more slowly, but more efficiently, is by far the predominant Power.
scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants

label: Individual differences supply the material for natural selection
statement: The slight individual differences among members of a species provide the materials that natural selection accumulates, in the same way that man accumulates individual differences in domestic productions.
quote: These individual differences are highly important for us, as they afford materials for natural selection to accumulate, in the same manner as man can accumulate in any given direction individual differences in his domesticated productions.
scope: species in a state of nature

label: Polymorphic genera vary in traits of no use, unfixed by selection
statement: In polymorphic genera such as Rubus, Rosa and Hieracium, the inordinate variation concerns structures that are of no service or disservice to the species and so have not been seized on and made definite by natural selection.
quote: I am inclined to suspect that we see in these polymorphic genera variations in points of structure which are of no service or disservice to the species, and which consequently have not been seized on and rendered definite by natural selection
scope: polymorphic genera of plants, insects and brachiopods

label: Doubtful forms of mobile animals are rare within a country but common between areas
statement: Among highly locomotive animals that unite for each birth, doubtful forms ranked as species by some and varieties by others are rarely found within the same country but are common in separated areas.
quote: Amongst animals which unite for each birth, and which are highly locomotive, doubtful forms, ranked by one zoologist as a species and by another as a variety, can rarely be found within the same country, but are common in separated areas.
scope: highly mobile sexually reproducing animals such as birds and insects

label: No clear line separates species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences
statement: No clear line of demarcation exists between species and sub-species, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences; they blend into one another in an insensible series.
quote: Certainly no clear line of demarcation has as yet been drawn between species and sub-species—that is, the forms which in the opinion of some naturalists come very near to, but do not quite arrive at the rank of species; or, again, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences.
scope: plants and animals in nature

label: Natural selection turns slight varieties into more distinct ones and species
statement: Individual differences lead to slight varieties, these to more distinct and permanent varieties, then to sub-species and species, the passage being mainly due to natural selection accumulating structural differences in definite directions, so that a well-marked variety is an incipient species.
quote: I attribute the passage of a variety, from a state in which it differs very slightly from its parent to one in which it differs more, to the action of natural selection in accumulating (as will hereafter be more fully explained) differences of structure in certain definite directions.
scope: varieties and species in nature

label: The term species is arbitrary and not essentially different from variety
statement: The term species is given arbitrarily, for convenience, to a set of closely resembling individuals and does not differ essentially from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.
quote: I look at the term species, as one arbitrarily given for the sake of convenience to a set of individuals closely resembling each other, and that it does not essentially differ from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.
scope: taxonomic practice for all organisms

label: Dominant species, widespread and abundant, produce the most varieties
statement: The dominant species, those that range widely over the world, are most diffused in their own country and are most numerous in individuals, most often produce well-marked varieties.
quote: Hence it is the most flourishing, or, as they may be called, the dominant species,—those which range widely over the world, are the most diffused in their own country, and are the most numerous in individuals,—which oftenest produce well-marked varieties, or, as I consider them, incipient species.
scope: plants in regional floras

label: Species of larger genera more often present varieties
statement: Within a country, a larger proportion of the species in larger genera present varieties than of the species in smaller genera, and those that vary have on average more varieties.
quote: it has invariably proved to be the case that a larger proportion of the species on the side of the larger genera present varieties, than on the side of the smaller genera.
scope: plants of regional floras and beetles of local faunas

label: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish
statement: Over geological time small genera have often increased greatly in number of species, and large genera have often reached a maximum, declined and disappeared.
quote: geology plainly tells us that small genera have in the lapse of time often increased greatly in size; and that large genera have often come to their maxima, declined, and disappeared.
scope: genera in the fossil record

label: Where many species of a genus have formed, many are still forming
statement: On the view that species are strongly marked varieties, where many species of a genus have been formed, on average many new species should still be forming.
quote: All that we want to show is, that where many species of a genus have been formed, on an average many are still forming; and this holds good.
scope: genera of plants and animals

label: Species in large genera differ from one another by small amounts
statement: In large genera the amount of difference between species is often exceedingly small, so that their species resemble varieties more than do species of small genera.
quote: Now Fries has remarked in regard to plants, and Westwood in regard to insects, that in large genera the amount of difference between the species is often exceedingly small. I have endeavoured to test this numerically by averages, and, as far as my imperfect results go, they always confirm the view.
scope: plant and insect genera

label: Species of large genera cluster unequally around certain species
statement: Species of large genera are not equally distinct from one another but are clustered in little groups around certain other species, as varieties are clustered around their parent species.
quote: As Fries has well remarked, little groups of species are generally clustered like satellites around certain other species.
scope: species within large genera

label: Species very closely allied to others have restricted ranges, like varieties
statement: Species that are very closely allied to other species, and so resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges, similar to the restricted ranges of acknowledged varieties.
quote: But there is also reason to believe, that those species which are very closely allied to other species, and in so far resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges.
scope: plants (British flora), extended to species generally

label: Analogies between species of large genera and varieties support descent
statement: The analogies between species of large genera and varieties (more varieties, small and unequal differences, restricted ranges) are understandable if species once existed as varieties, and inexplicable if each species was independently created.
quote: And we can clearly understand these analogies, if species have once existed as varieties, and have thus originated: whereas, these analogies are utterly inexplicable if each species has been independently created.
scope: species and varieties of plants and animals

label: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant
statement: Because the dominant species of larger genera vary most and varieties become new species, larger genera tend to become larger, and dominant forms tend to become more dominant by leaving many modified, dominant descendants.
quote: The larger genera thus tend to become larger; and throughout nature the forms of life which are now dominant tend to become still more dominant by leaving many modified and dominant descendants.
scope: genera and dominant species throughout nature

label: Overproduction makes a struggle for existence inevitable
statement: Because all organisms tend to increase at a high (geometrical) rate, more individuals are produced than can survive, so every species must undergo a struggle for existence with members of its own species, with other species, or with physical conditions.
quote: A struggle for existence inevitably follows from the high rate at which all organic beings tend to increase.
scope: all plants and animals in a state of nature

label: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species
statement: The extraordinarily rapid increase and wide spread of introduced (naturalised) animals and plants in new countries is explained by geometrical increase under favourable conditions with reduced mortality, not by any rise in their fertility.
quote: In such cases the geometrical ratio of increase, the result of which never fails to be surprising, simply explains the extraordinarily rapid increase and wide diffusion of naturalised productions in their new homes.
scope: introduced and feral animals and plants

label: Average abundance depends only indirectly on fecundity
statement: The average number of individuals of an animal or plant species depends only indirectly on how many eggs or seeds it produces; high fecundity mainly compensates for heavy destruction, usually early in life.
quote: So that in all cases, the average number of any animal or plant depends only indirectly on the number of its eggs or seeds.
scope: all animals and plants

label: Predation, more often than food supply, sets average numbers
statement: Although food sets the upper limit to a species' increase, very often it is destruction by predators rather than food supply that determines the species' average numbers.
quote: The amount of food for each species of course gives the extreme limit to which each can increase; but very frequently it is not the obtaining food, but the serving as prey to other animals, which determines the average numbers of a species.
scope: animal populations in nature, e.g. game birds and mammals

label: Periodic extreme cold or drought is the most effective check
statement: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodic seasons of extreme cold or drought are the most effective of all checks on increase.
quote: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodical seasons of extreme cold or drought, I believe to be the most effective of all checks.
scope: animal and plant populations, e.g. birds in severe winters

label: Competitors decline poleward, so climate acts more directly there
statement: The number of species, and therefore of competitors, decreases going northward, so that going north or up a mountain one more often finds stunted forms caused by the direct harmful action of climate than going south or downhill.
quote: for the number of species of all kinds, and therefore of competitors, decreases northwards; hence in going northward, or in ascending a mountain, we far oftener meet with stunted forms, due to the _directly_ injurious action of climate, than we do in proceeding southwards or in descending a mountain.
scope: plants and animals along latitudinal and elevational gradients

label: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring competitors
statement: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring their competitors and enemies; for example, many garden plants that tolerate the local climate never become naturalised because they cannot compete with native plants or resist native animals.
quote: That climate acts in main part indirectly by favouring other species, we may clearly see in the prodigious number of plants in our gardens which can perfectly well endure our climate, but which never become naturalised, for they cannot compete with our native plants, nor resist destruction by our native animals.
scope: plants, especially cultivated exotics and native floras

label: Many species need a large local stock to persist
statement: In many cases a large number of individuals of a species, relative to the number of its enemies, is necessary for the species to survive, which explains why rare plants can be very abundant in the few spots where they occur.
quote: On the other hand, in many cases, a large stock of individuals of the same species, relatively to the numbers of its enemies, is absolutely necessary for its preservation.
scope: plants and animals subject to predation, e.g. seed crops eaten by birds

label: Balanced struggles keep communities uniform over long periods
statement: Although competition between organisms constantly recurs with shifting outcomes, the opposing forces are so finely balanced that community composition stays roughly the same for long periods, even though a trifling change could tip the balance toward one organism.
quote: Battle within battle must ever be recurring with varying success; and yet in the long-run the forces are so nicely balanced, that the face of nature remains uniform for long periods of time, though assuredly the merest trifle would often give the victory to one organic being over another.
scope: natural communities of plants and animals

label: Chains of interaction link distant species' abundances
statement: Very different organisms are linked by chains of interaction, so that the abundance of one species can determine the frequency of another through intermediate species; for example, cats may control the frequency of red clover and heartsease by way of field-mice and humble-bees.
quote: Hence it is quite credible that the presence of a feline animal in large numbers in a district might determine, through the intervention first of mice and then of bees, the frequency of certain flowers in that district!
scope: terrestrial communities of plants, pollinators, and their predators

label: Struggle is most severe between members of the same species
statement: The struggle for existence is almost always most severe between individuals of the same species, because they live in the same places, need the same food and face the same dangers; between varieties of a species it is nearly as severe.
quote: But the struggle almost invariably will be most severe between the individuals of the same species, for they frequent the same districts, require the same food, and are exposed to the same dangers.
scope: all organisms, including varieties of cultivated plants and domestic animals

label: Congeners compete more severely than species of different genera
statement: Because species of the same genus are usually similar in habits and constitution and always in structure, competition between them is generally more severe than between species of different genera.
quote: As species of the same genus have usually, though by no means invariably, some similarity in habits and constitution, and always in structure, the struggle will generally be more severe between species of the same genus, when they come into competition with each other, than between species of distinct genera.
scope: co-occurring species of plants and animals

label: Each organism's structure is shaped by its relations to other organisms
statement: The structure of every organism is related, in essential but often hidden ways, to the structure of the other organisms with which it competes, from which it must escape, or on which it preys.
quote: A corollary of the highest importance may be deduced from the foregoing remarks, namely, that the structure of every organic being is related, in the most essential yet often hidden manner, to that of all other organic beings, with which it comes into competition for food or residence, or from which it has to escape, or on which it preys.
scope: all organisms

label: Few species reach range edges where climate alone kills them
statement: Only a few plants or animals extend their ranges so far that they are destroyed by the severity of climate alone; competition continues everywhere except at the extreme limits of life.
quote: we have reason to believe that only a few plants or animals range so far, that they are destroyed by the rigour of the climate alone.
scope: geographic range limits of plants and animals

label: Natural selection preserves favourable and destroys injurious variations
statement: Because more individuals are born than can survive, individuals with any advantage, however slight, have the best chance of surviving and reproducing, while injurious variations are eliminated; this preservation of favourable and rejection of injurious variations is natural selection.
quote: This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.
scope: all organisms in nature

label: Neutral variations escape selection and remain fluctuating
statement: Variations that are neither useful nor harmful are not acted on by natural selection and stay variable, which may explain the variability of so-called polymorphic species.
quote: Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.
scope: characters of all organisms, especially polymorphic species

label: No native biota is so well adapted that it cannot be improved
statement: No country's native inhabitants are so perfectly adapted that none could be improved, as shown by introduced species having established firmly in every country.
quote: No country can be named in which all the native inhabitants are now so perfectly adapted to each other and to the physical conditions under which they live, that none of them could anyhow be improved; for in all countries, the natives have been so far conquered by naturalised productions, that they have allowed foreigners to take firm possession of the land.
scope: native biotas of all countries and regions

label: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection
statement: Seemingly trivial characters such as colour can be shaped by natural selection; colours that match the background, as in green leaf-eating insects and heather-coloured grouse, protect their bearers from predators that hunt by sight.
quote: When we see leaf-eating insects green, and bark-feeders mottled-grey; the alpine ptarmigan white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather, and the black-grouse that of peaty earth, we must believe that these tints are of service to these birds and insects in preserving them from danger.
scope: animals preyed on by visually hunting predators

label: Natural selection can modify organisms at any age
statement: Because variations arising at a particular life stage tend to be inherited at the same stage, natural selection can modify organisms at any age, for instance adapting larvae independently of adults.
quote: natural selection will be enabled to act on and modify organic beings at any age, by the accumulation of profitable variations at that age, and by their inheritance at a corresponding age.
scope: all organisms, especially those with distinct life stages such as insects with larvae

label: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons
statement: Fighting between males for females is perhaps most severe in polygamous animals, and the males of such species are the most often equipped with special weapons.
quote: The war is, perhaps, severest between the males of polygamous animals, and these seem oftenest provided with special weapons.
scope: animals with male-male competition for mates, especially mammals and birds

label: Female choice over many generations can produce male ornaments
statement: Female birds, by choosing the most melodious or beautiful males over thousands of generations, can produce a marked change in male song or plumage.
quote: I can see no good reason to doubt that female birds, by selecting, during thousands of generations, the most melodious or beautiful males, according to their standard of beauty, might produce a marked effect.
scope: birds, especially species with male display

label: Sex differences in species with shared habits are mainly sexually selected
statement: When males and females of a species share the same general habits of life but differ in structure, colour or ornament, those differences were mainly caused by sexual selection, although not all such differences are.
quote: Thus it is, as I believe, that when the males and females of any animal have the same general habits of life, but differ in structure, colour, or ornament, such differences have been mainly caused by sexual selection
scope: sexually dimorphic animals

label: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted
statement: A flower and a bee can slowly become modified and adapted to each other, at the same time or one after the other, by the continued preservation of individuals with mutually favourable slight differences in structure.
quote: Thus I can understand how a flower and a bee might slowly become, either simultaneously or one after the other, modified and adapted in the most perfect manner to each other, by the continued preservation of individuals presenting mutual and slightly favourable deviations of structure.
scope: flowering plants and their insect pollinators

label: Natural selection works only by accumulating very small modifications
statement: Natural selection acts only by preserving and accumulating very small inherited modifications, each profitable to its bearer, and so excludes continued creation of new organisms or large sudden changes of structure.
quote: Natural selection can act only by the preservation and accumulation of infinitesimally small inherited modifications, each profitable to the preserved being
scope: all organisms

label: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it
statement: In animals and plants, crosses between different varieties or between different strains of the same variety give vigour and fertility to the offspring, while close interbreeding reduces vigour and fertility.
quote: a cross between different varieties, or between individuals of the same variety but of another strain, gives vigour and fertility to the offspring; and on the other hand, that _close_ interbreeding diminishes vigour and fertility
scope: animals and plants, wild and domestic

label: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed
statement: It is a general law of nature that no organism fertilises itself for an unlimited number of generations; an occasional cross with another individual, perhaps at long intervals, is indispensable, even in hermaphrodites.
quote: it is a general law of nature (utterly ignorant though we be of the meaning of the law) that no organic being self-fertilises itself for an eternity of generations; but that a cross with another individual is occasionally—perhaps at very long intervals—indispensable.
scope: all plants and animals, especially hermaphrodites

label: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants
statement: Trees, across all plant orders, have separate male and female flowers more often than other plants do, which helps pollen move between trees (though Hooker reported the rule fails in Australia).
quote: That trees belonging to all Orders have their sexes more often separated than other plants, I find to be the case in this country
scope: flowering plants, comparing trees with non-woody plants

label: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations
statement: A large number of individuals favours natural selection because it gives a better chance for profitable variations to arise within a given period, compensating for lower variability in each individual.
quote: A large number of individuals, by giving a better chance for the appearance within any given period of profitable variations, will compensate for a lesser amount of variability in each individual, and is, I believe, an extremely important element of success.
scope: all species undergoing natural selection

label: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species
statement: Although small isolated areas can favour new species, modification is generally faster on large areas, and forms produced there, having beaten many competitors, spread most widely and give rise to the most new varieties and species.
quote: Finally, I conclude that, although small isolated areas probably have been in some respects highly favourable for the production of new species, yet that the course of modification will generally have been more rapid on large areas; and what is more important, that the new forms produced on large areas, which already have been victorious over many competitors, will be those that will spread most widely
scope: terrestrial species in continents versus islands and small regions

label: Freshwater biotas evolve and go extinct more slowly, keeping relict forms
statement: Because all freshwater basins together form a small area, competition among freshwater organisms has been less severe, so new forms have arisen more slowly and old forms have been exterminated more slowly there, which is why fresh water holds ancient and anomalous forms.
quote: All fresh-water basins, taken together, make a small area compared with that of the sea or of the land; and, consequently, the competition between fresh-water productions will have been less severe than elsewhere; new forms will have been more slowly formed, and old forms more slowly exterminated.
scope: freshwater organisms, compared with marine and terrestrial ones

label: Natural selection acts slowly, intermittently and on few species at a time
statement: Natural selection always acts very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of a region at the same time.
quote: On the other hand, I do believe that natural selection will always act very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of the same region at the same time.
scope: all organisms within a region over geological time

label: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction
statement: Because every area is already fully stocked, as a favoured form increases in number the less favoured forms decrease and become rare, and rarity precedes extinction.
quote: it follows that as each selected and favoured form increases in number, so will the less favoured forms decrease and become rare. Rarity, as geology tells us, is the precursor to extinction.
scope: species in fully occupied areas, over ecological and geological time

label: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives
statement: Because the most closely related forms compete most severely, each new variety or species, while forming, presses hardest on its nearest relatives and tends to exterminate them.
quote: Consequently, each new variety or species, during the progress of its formation, will generally press hardest on its nearest kindred, and tend to exterminate them.
scope: varieties and species, wild and domesticated

label: Divergence of character maximises the life an area supports
statement: The greatest amount of life can be supported in an area by great diversification of structure among its inhabitants.
quote: The truth of the principle, that the greatest amount of life can be supported by great diversification of structure, is seen under many natural circumstances.
scope: local communities of plants and animals

label: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders
statement: Where organisms compete most closely, as on a small patch of ground, the advantages of diversification mean that the coexisting inhabitants generally belong to different genera and orders.
quote: where they come into the closest competition with each other, the advantages of diversification of structure, with the accompanying differences of habit and constitution, determine that the inhabitants, which thus jostle each other most closely, shall, as a general rule, belong to what we call different genera and orders.
scope: small-area communities, e.g. turf plots, islets, small ponds

label: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
statement: Floras gain far more new genera than new species from naturalised plants, relative to the native numbers of genera and species, so naturalised plants tend to differ from the natives at the genus level.
quote: floras gain by naturalisation, proportionally with the number of the native genera and species, far more in new genera than in new species.
scope: naturalised plants in regional floras

label: Intermediate forms and parent species tend to go extinct
statement: In a fully stocked country, improved descendants of a species tend to supplant their predecessors, so the intermediate forms between earlier and later states, and the original parent species itself, generally tend to become extinct.
quote: Hence all the intermediate forms between the earlier and later states, that is between the less and more improved state of a species, as well as the original parent-species itself, will generally tend to become extinct.
scope: lineages of species descended from a common parent

label: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups
statement: Extinct species, though generally in the same orders, families or genera as living ones, are often somewhat intermediate in character between existing groups, because they lived when the branching lines of descent had diverged less.
quote: the diagram throws light on the affinities of extinct beings, which, though generally belonging to the same orders, or families, or genera, with those now living, yet are often, in some degree, intermediate in character between existing groups
scope: fossil and living species of all groups
